articles.title: I Asked My Git Repository What It Remembered - and Found a Ghost 👻
articles.excerpt: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine. A repository can forget a feature without losing its fingerprints. I know the feeling of opening an ol…
articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine . What I Built A repository can forget a feature without losing its fingerprints. I know the feeling of opening an old project, spotting a strange workaround, and wondering: Why on earth did we do it this way? The person who wrote it might have moved on. The documentation might be missing. But buried underneath today's code is a quieter version of the project - one preserved commit at a time. So I built RepoGhost , a local AI archaeologist that helps developers explore their project's forgotten history. Instead of creating a fictional ghost that makes things up, it listens to the ghosts we already have: real Git commits .

articles.title: Supabase's 30 Oct change: the next table your AI builder creates needs a GRANT. Here's the 2-minute check.
articles.excerpt: If your app was built with Lovable, Bolt or another AI builder on top of Supabase, one thing changes on 30 October 2026: new tables stop being reachable from your app until they get an explicit Postgr…
articles.body: If your app was built with Lovable, Bolt or another AI builder on top of Supabase, one thing changes on 30 October 2026 : new tables stop being reachable from your app until they get an explicit Postgres GRANT . Your existing tables keep working. The one that breaks is the next table, for example when you ask your AI builder for a new feature on 31 Oct. Everything below is from Supabase's own changelog and docs, read on 28 Oct 2026. We haven't run the change on a test project. What changes Until now, Supabase granted select , insert , update and delete on every new table in the public schema to the anon , authenticated and service_role roles, so a table was reachable through the Data API (the REST/GraphQL layer that supabase-js calls) the moment it existed.

articles.excerpt: Liberation I'm not talking about the length of package.json files. I run into those far too often in my daily work. What I'm talking about is how, lately, new barriers seem to be falling almost every…
articles.body: Liberation I'm not talking about the length of package.json files. I run into those far too often in my daily work. What I'm talking about is how, lately, new barriers seem to be falling almost every week. Until recently, we used the programming languages and technologies we already knew to solve problems. But over the past six months, this has changed dramatically. You no longer need to stay within your comfort zone. You can use practically any technology you want. The focus of software development has shifted from - How do I build it? to - What should I build? And we need much smaller development teams. Sometimes a single developer is enough, suddenly finding themselves in the role of a software architect. Of course, smaller teams also mean greater responsibility.

articles.title: Checkout Totals: Why the Server Recalculates Every Time, Not Once
articles.excerpt: A checkout page shows a subtotal, a VAT line, a total. Somewhere in the request that submits the order, a server-side checkout total calculation has to confirm those numbers are correct before chargin…
articles.body: A checkout page shows a subtotal, a VAT line, a total. Somewhere in the request that submits the order, a server-side checkout total calculation has to confirm those numbers are correct before charging a card. The wrong answer to ‘where does that decision happen’ is a well-known exploit category: if the server trusts a total the client sent along with the order, changing that total is a browser dev-tools exercise, not a hack. The right answer is simple: the server recomputes the total from its own product data, every time, on every order, rather than accepting a total the client already computed. What needs unpacking is what that requires once the storefront sells in multiple markets, multiple currencies, and multiple VAT regimes.

articles.body: TL;DR Bank of America is warning customers not to share banking usernames or passwords with AI assistants and agents. Customers could be held responsible for activity resulting from voluntarily granting an AI agent account access, subject to applicable consumer protections. As Gemini, Claude, ChatGPT, and other AI assistants become more autonomous, banks are increasingly concerned about unauthorized access and liability. AI assistants can write your emails, book appointments, shop on your behalf, and increasingly handle tasks you’d rather not do yourself. articles.title: Black holes can split in two — but only if they spin at extreme speeds
articles.excerpt: Scientists have long known that when two black holes collide, they merge to create a more massive black hole. New research suggests that the opposite may happen too: single black holes may split in tw…
articles.body: Scientists have long known that when two black holes collide, they merge to create a more massive black hole. These events are so violent that they set the very fabric of space ringing with ripples called gravitational waves. Now, new research suggests that the opposite may happen, too: single black holes may be able to split in two. But this can only happen if that progenitor black hole is spinning at maximum possible speed. That speed prevents the black holes from immediately falling back on each other. There are physical laws in place that would usually prevent black holes from splitting in two; the team behind this research investigated whether there are conditions in which these laws can be temporarily bypassed.

articles.title: How 'spacewalking' underwater made me feel like I was really in space
articles.excerpt: Analog Astronaut Commander and Aquanaut Michaela Musilova led underwater simulated “spacewalks” in low visibility to test astronaut safety and communication protocols during simulated space missions.
articles.body: I was breathing just fine through my life support systems, but I kept feeling an urge to double check that everything was ok with my "spacesuit" before heading out on this "spacewalk." I have worn many different types of spacesuits on Earth during my career, but for the first time in my life, I knew that I couldn’t just stop to breathe the air outside if there were an emergency. That's because I was underwater. On this excursion, I was leading a simulated space mission underwater called SEA STAR. My " spacesuit " was actually scuba diving gear, and the simulated spacewalks , or EVAs (Extra-Vehicular Activities), included outings where we explored underwater environments.
